title: 5T OTA
description: The five-transistor OTA, biased from the TAIL NODE and entered from the COMMON MODE. Internally the tail node is the one free bias variable: the pair's source sits at $V_{tail}$, so both of its transistors have $V_{tail}$ as their body bias and a drain-source voltage measured up from it — to the output on one side, to the load's diode node on the other — and every device is read straight out of the table. The currents are stated the way the circuit sets them: only the bias reference is programmed, with $I_{tail}$; the tail device shares that reference's gate and width, so what it delivers is $I_{tail}$ less the mirror's drain-voltage error; the pair's output-side transistor carries its share of what the tail delivers, and its partner is the same width on the same gate-source voltage with its drain on the load's diode side, so its current is read from the table at that drain; the load's diode side carries what that partner passes; and the load mirror's output side shares its diode side's gate, so the two sides differ by their drain voltages in the same way. The share is the one thing solved besides the tail node: with the inputs balanced the pair's two currents have to add up to what the tail delivers, and wherever the output does not sit one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply the pair's two drains differ, so the split is not one half each. The mirror's two drains differ there as well, and the current the two differences leave missing at the output is reported as a systematic input offset. Held fixed and asked about at another process condition, the design therefore moves as the silicon would — one programmed current, with every other device following it through a shared gate or a shared node. Externally the designer types the common mode the application presents: $CM_{in} = V_{tail} + V_{GS}$ rises monotonically with the tail node, so the engine searches $V_{tail}$ inside its stated range until the produced common mode equals $CM_{dc}$ — a search that keeps the answer enclosed and owes nothing to a starting guess. Sweep $CM_{dc}$ to trace the common-mode axis. Gain falls as the common mode rises, because lifting the tail node squeezes the pair's own $v_{ds}$ — and it collapses well before the pair leaves saturation, which is why the gain check, not a saturation edge, sets the usable ceiling.

params.name: vn_target
params.note: input-referred thermal density budget, set above the 28 nV/rtHz floor measured on a sky130 tt realization of this OTA rather than above the gamma-model row (22.6 nV/rtHz there at the default 20 uA and gm/ID split, the pair receiving a little under the programmed current). Clearing only the model is how a spec looks closable and is not; tighten this and the sweep shows what the noise really costs

params.name: vos_target
params.note: input offset budget, 1 sigma. Half-micron devices at 20 uA are SMALL (about 1.8 um x 0.5 um here), so the generic Pelgrom coefficient puts the spread near 9 mV — offset is the 5T's area tax, and shrinking this budget is what forces bigger devices. The systematic part is reported on its own row and is not charged against this budget

params.name: CM_lo
params.note: input CM range the application presents, low edge. The cm-lo edge re-evaluates the whole sheet here, so this claim is CHECKED at every evaluation, on the design this run produced — the sweep shows the widest range that would close (from 0.96 V up to the 1.45 V top of the CM_dc slider on sky130 tt at the shipped choices). The edge checks the ENDPOINT; the interior is the sweep's to show

params.name: CM_hi
params.note: input CM range the application presents, high edge — its ENDPOINT checked by the cm-hi edge the same way

params.name: CM_dc
params.note: the input common mode the application presents. The engine places the tail node so the sheet sits exactly here; sweep it to trace the common-mode axis

params.name: V_out_dc
params.note: output DC level; sets the mirror output device's vds and the top of the output-side pair transistor's vds. That transistor's drain and the mirror output device's drain meet at a high-impedance output that nothing on this sheet holds; the feedback the application closes around the amplifier holds it here. Wherever that is not one diode drop below the supply, the two sides of the load mirror carry different currents and so do the two transistors of the pair, and the systematic-offset row reports what that costs

params.name: avt
params.note: Pelgrom A_VT

params.name: abeta
params.note: Pelgrom A_beta

params.name: V_tail
params.note: the tail node — the design's one free bias variable, solved rather than set: the engine searches between min and max (the range it is searched in, not slider bounds) until the produced common mode equals CM_dc. It fixes the pair's body bias and both of its drain-source voltages in one stroke; the shown value is where it landed. An end of the range where the relation does not evaluate is stepped inward silently, and the searched range is reported only if the search then fails. Its partner is read from the table, not sized, so the high end may sit above the load's diode node without stopping the solve

params.name: out_share
params.note: the share of the tail current the pair's output-side transistor carries with the inputs balanced — solved, not set. The pair's two transistors are one width on one gate-source voltage, but one drain is the output and the other the load's diode node, so they do not carry equal currents and the tail current does not split in half. The engine searches for the share at which this equals the output-side transistor's fraction of the pair's current as the table reads the two (the pair_split row), which is the current law at the tail node: the two currents add up to what the tail delivers. The stored value is never read. It is searched between 0.01 and 0.99, a share of the tail current that leaves each transistor some of it

params.name: I_tail
params.note: the current the bias reference is programmed to — the one current on this sheet that is typed. The tail device mirrors it 1:1 through the shared gate and delivers it less the mirror's drain-voltage error (the tail node normally sits below the reference's diode drop); slew rate, bandwidth and supply current are computed from what is delivered, not from this number

params.name: gm_id_in
params.note: input-pair inversion, set on the output-side transistor; its partner sits at the same gate-source voltage. Sets gm per current, noise, and the CM-low edge

params.name: gm_id_ld
params.note: mirror-load inversion, set on the diode side and inherited by the output side through the shared gate: lower gm/ID adds less noise and offset (both scale with the load's gm)

params.name: gm_id_tail
params.note: inversion level of the bias reference, which the tail device inherits through the shared gate: higher V* costs CM-low headroom

params.name: L_tail
params.note: length of the bias reference and of the tail device, which mirror at one length: longer shrinks the mirror's drain-voltage error

params.name: ld_sign
params.note: vds sign convention of the load table: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis. Only the output side reads it — the diode side's drain follows its own gate in whichever convention its table uses. Read both sides of the mirror from the same table: the gate voltage they share is passed in that table's convention

doc.title: Tail bias reference
doc.description: The diode-connected reference the programmed current $I_{tail}$ flows into — the one device on this sheet whose current is typed. Its drain is its gate, so its $V_{DS}$ is its own $V_{GS}$ and the table is read along that diagonal with nothing estimated. It publishes its width and its gate voltage, which is all the tail device needs to copy it.

doc.title: Tail current source
doc.description: The tail device, on the bias reference's gate at the reference's width: a 1:1 mirror of the programmed current, with the tail node as its drain-source voltage. Its current is read off the table rather than typed — the reference sits at its own diode drop and this device at $V_{tail}$, so it delivers the programmed current scaled by what that difference in $V_{DS}$ does through its $g_{ds}$. It leaves saturation when $V_{tail}$ falls below its own $V_{dsat}$, which is what sets the low end of the usable common-mode range.

params.name: W_t
params.note: the bias reference's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgs_t
params.note: the bias reference's gate voltage — the gate wire the two share

params.name: vds_t
params.note: the tail node

doc.title: Input-pair device, output side
doc.description: The pair transistor whose drain is the output, sized at its share of what the tail delivers. The pair's two transistors share a gate drive and a source but not a drain, so the tail current does not split evenly between them, and this is the one whose $g_{ds}$ loads the output. Both of its bias coordinates come from the tail node directly: the source sits at $V_{tail}$, so that is its body bias, and its drain-source voltage is what is left between the output level and that source. It publishes its width and its gate-source voltage, which is all its partner on the diode side needs to copy it.

doc.title: Mirror-load device, diode side
doc.description: The diode-connected side of the mirror load. It carries the current of the pair transistor above it — what the tail delivers less the output-side transistor's share — and its drain is its gate, so it sits one $V_{GS}$ below the supply whatever the output does. That gate is the mirror node: this device's $g_m$ sets the second pole, its width and gate voltage are what the output side copies, and its drain is where the pair transistor in the same branch has its own.

doc.title: Input-pair device, diode side
doc.description: The pair transistor whose drain is the load's diode node: the output-side transistor's width on the output-side transistor's gate-source voltage, which is what a matched pair with balanced inputs on a common source is. Its body bias is the tail node, like its partner's, but its drain sits one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply instead of at the output, so its current is read off the table at that drain, not typed. Wherever the two drains differ it carries a different current than its partner, and the split of the tail current between the two is solved so that they add up to what the tail delivers.

params.name: W_i
params.note: the output-side transistor's width — a matched pair

params.name: vgs_i
params.note: the output-side transistor's gate-source voltage — balanced inputs on the source node the two share

params.name: vds_i
params.note: from the tail node up to the load's diode node

doc.title: Mirror-load device, output side
doc.description: The output side of the mirror load, on the diode side's gate at the diode side's width. The output node and the supply set its drain, so the input common mode reaches it only through the small change in tail current that its diode side passes on, and its $g_{ds}$ is all but fixed once the output level is chosen. Its current is read off the table at that drain voltage rather than typed: wherever the output does not sit one diode drop below the supply it differs from the diode side's, and that difference is the mirror's part of the systematic offset the sheet reports.

params.name: W_l
params.note: the diode side's width — a 1:1 copy

params.name: vgs_l
params.note: the diode side's gate voltage — the mirror node the two share, in the sign convention of the diode side's table

params.name: vds_l
params.note: output-side vds, signed to this table's axis convention

equations.name: CM_in
equations.note: the input common mode this bias produces — an OUTPUT here, not a setting. It rises monotonically with the tail node — which is why the pin that places the tail node from $CM_{dc}$ is a well-posed one-unknown search

equations.name: pair_split
equations.note: the fraction of the pair's current that its output-side transistor carries with the inputs balanced and the output at $V_{out,dc}$, as the table reads the two — what out_share is solved to. One half when the output sits one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply; above one half when the output is higher than that, because the output-side transistor then has the larger drain-source voltage, and below it when the output is lower

equations.name: gm_pair
equations.note: the pair's differential transconductance: a differential input sees the two transistors in series through their common source, so this is the series combination of their two $g_m$, doubled — either transistor's own $g_m$ when the two are equal

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: the resistance this OTA presents at its output — the two output-node conductances in parallel, the output-side pair transistor's and the mirror output device's, both read at $V_{out,dc}$. The gain below assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this row is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

equations.name: Av
equations.note: differential gain: the pair's transconductance into the two output conductances, both read at the OUTPUT node $V_{out,dc}$ — the drain that actually loads the gain. Raising the tail node squeezes the pair's $v_{ds}$, so gain falls as the common mode rises

equations.name: GBW
equations.note: dominant-pole gain-bandwidth into the load, from the pair's transconductance

equations.name: f_pole
equations.note: estimate: the mirror-node pole, the diode side's $g_m$ over both mirror gates' $C_{GG}$; the 5T's second pole. Read on the diode side, the device whose $g_m$ is that node's conductance

equations.name: PM
equations.note: estimate: phase margin left after the mirror node. That node is a pole-ZERO DOUBLET, not a lone pole — only half the signal takes the mirror path, putting a zero at twice the pole — so it costs far less phase than $f_{pole}$ alone suggests

equations.name: SR
equations.note: the whole tail current steered into the load — the current the tail device delivers, not the number the reference is programmed to

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: both pair transistors and both mirror devices contribute, each at its own density: vn_inr^2 + vn_in^2 + (vn_ldr*gm_ldr/gm_pair)^2 + (vn_ld*gm_ld/gm_pair)^2. A pair transistor's noise is in series with its own input, so it enters as it is; a mirror device's is a current at the output, referred back through the pair's transconductance. Each side of the pair and of the mirror is read separately because the two sides sit at different drain voltages; counting all four devices is the simulation-verified two-sided total

equations.name: vos
equations.expr: sqrt((pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, in__W, L_in, inr__gm/inr__id)^2 + pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, in__W, L_in, in__gm/in__id)^2)/2 + (pelgrom_vos(avt, abeta, ldr__W, L_ld, gm_id_ld)*ldr__gm/gm_pair)^2)
equations.note: random offset, 1 sigma: the input pair's offset plus the mirror pair's offset referred through the pair's transconductance. Each pair transistor contributes half of a matched pair's variance at its own gm/ID — the two share a width and a gate-source voltage but not a drain. The mirror pair is read at the diode side, whose width the output side copies

equations.name: vos_sys
equations.note: estimate: input-referred systematic offset — the current missing at the output node with the inputs balanced, over the pair's transconductance: what the output-side pair transistor takes, less what the mirror's output side returns. Two differences are in it, both read from the table. The pair's two transistors share a width and a gate-source voltage, but the diode-side drain sits one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply and the output-side drain at $V_{out,dc}$, so the output side takes a different current than its partner passes on to the mirror's diode side. The mirror's output side shares the diode side's gate but sits at $V_{DD} - V_{out,dc}$ while the diode side sits at its own diode drop, so it returns a different current than the diode side receives. The two differences always push the output the same way, and both are zero when the output sits one load $V_{GS}$ below the supply. With $V_{out,dc}$ held by a loop outside this sheet, the missing current has to come from an input imbalance of this size. Reported only; no check reads it

equations.name: tail_headroom
equations.note: how far the tail node sits above the tail device's saturation edge — exact here, because the tail node is the variable rather than something inferred from a common mode

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance one input terminal presents — the gate capacitance of a single pair transistor, as the mean of the two, which differ a little because their drains do. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it, so a driving stage sees more than this. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current of the amplifier — the current the tail device delivers is the whole of it, because the mirror load carries that same current down from the supply. The reference branch that programs it is shared bias infrastructure, typically one reference feeding several stages, and is not counted here. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no rule reads it

checks.note: estimate: margin left at crossover once the mirror doublet is paid for; advisory, since an open-loop OTA needs none of it and sim owns the real stability
computed from the gamma-model floor; this table carries no measured noise; the simulator owns noise sign-off
below this the tail source drops out of saturation and the bias current collapses; this is the mechanism behind the low end of the common-mode range
the common mode this bias produces has to sit inside the range the application presents
paired with cm-not-below. Sweep $CM_{dc}$ to see the whole span that closes — that span, not a saturation formula, is the common-mode range this design really supports

checks.lhs: min(VDD - abs(ldr__vgs) - V_tail - inr__vdsat, V_out_dc - V_tail - in__vdsat)
checks.justification: the pair's two drains sit at different levels — one a diode drop below the supply, the other at the output — so each transistor is held against its own saturation voltage and this watches whichever has less to spare. Gain collapses well before this trips, so treat it as a floor rather than as the usable ceiling
checks.note: trips when the tail node is pushed so high the pair runs out of drain-source voltage — lower V_tail, or spend less diode drop (lower gm_id_ld)

operatingRange.name: cm-lo
operatingRange.note: the claimed low edge, checked exactly: the whole sheet re-evaluates at CM_dc = CM_lo on the design this run produced — its own tail-node solve over its full range, every device held at the geometry it was sized to — and every hard rule must hold there. Replaces the linearized reach estimate this sheet used to carry

operatingRange.name: cm-hi
operatingRange.note: the claimed high edge, checked the same way. The edges check the ENDPOINTS; the interior is monotone for the saturation mechanisms here, and the CM_dc sweep remains the authority on the full landscape
